title.source: Section check: Who builds AI, and at what cost

intro.source: 8 questions about Lessons 5–8. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.0.question.source: Like clothes, an AI tool has a supply chain. What is a supply chain?

questions.0.options.0.text.source: The people who help make it, step by step

questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. A supply chain is all the people and places that help to make a product. Some of them stay hidden.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.note: “Some of them stay hidden” as “Một số người trong đó không được ai thấy” (no one sees some of them).

questions.0.options.1.text.source: A list of rules that say how the tool must work

questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Rules are not a supply chain. A supply chain is the people who help make a product. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.0.options.2.text.source: A shop where people can buy the tool

questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A shop sells a product. A supply chain is all the people who help to make it. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.1.question.source: In 2023, Oxford researchers checked 15 online work platforms. What did they find?

questions.1.options.0.text.source: Every platform paid all workers fairly

questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The researchers found low pay and a lot of unpaid time. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.1.options.1.text.source: Workers were paid for every hour they spent

questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. More than a quarter of the workers' time was unpaid, such as time looking for tasks. Look back at Lesson 5.

questions.1.options.2.text.source: None met all of their basic standards
questions.1.options.2.text.note: “None met all of their basic standards” as “Không nền tảng nào đạt đủ các tiêu chuẩn cơ bản”; Lesson 5's simpler text says “quy tắc cơ bản”, the standard text “tiêu chuẩn cơ bản”.

questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The best platform scored only 5 out of 10. Some platforms changed their rules after the study.

questions.2.question.source: Why do many data centres use water?

questions.2.options.0.text.source: To make the power that the chips use

questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Data centres use a lot of electricity, but the water does not make it. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.2.options.1.text.source: To cool chips that get very hot

questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. The chips use a lot of electricity and get very hot. Water helps to cool them.

questions.2.options.2.text.source: To wash the dust off the computers

questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The water is not for cleaning. It helps with the heat. Look back at Lesson 6.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.note: “It helps with the heat” as “Nó giúp hạ nhiệt” (it helps bring the heat down).

questions.3.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. A company plans a data centre in the made-up town of Westvale. It says about 800 people will help to build it over two years. About 40 people will work there after it opens.

questions.3.question.source: A man in the town says, “This will give 800 people work for years.” What is wrong with this?

questions.3.options.0.text.source: The building work lasts only two years

questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Building work ends when the building is finished. After that, there are only about 40 jobs.

questions.3.options.1.text.source: Data centres need nobody to build them

questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The company says about 800 people will help to build it. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.3.options.2.text.source: All 800 people will work inside it later

questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Only about 40 people will work there after it opens. Look back at Lesson 6.

questions.4.question.source: In Harbourside, few people publish books in Language C. What does “publish” mean?

questions.4.options.0.text.source: To speak a language at home

questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. People speak Language C a lot. To publish means to put out writing. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.4.options.1.text.source: To change words into another language

questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. That is to translate. To publish is to put out writing for many people. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.4.options.2.text.source: To put out writing for many to read
questions.4.options.2.text.note: Follows the Lesson 7 glossary definition of “xuất bản”.

questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. To publish is to print or put out writing. Little is published in Language C, so AI has little to learn from.

questions.5.question.source: Why do some languages have much more writing than others?

questions.5.options.0.text.source: Some languages are much harder to write

questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. It is not about how hard a language is. It depends on how a language has been used. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.5.options.1.text.source: History, such as which ones schools use

questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. It depends on history: which languages schools, books, news and governments use, and what people type online.

questions.5.options.2.text.source: The more speakers, the more writing

questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. In Harbourside, Language C has the most speakers but very little writing. Look back at Lesson 7.

questions.6.question.source: About 45% of a famous photo collection came from the United States, and about 2% from India. What does this help to explain?

questions.6.options.0.text.source: Why a tool did worse with photos from India

questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Few photos came from India, so the data did not represent it well. A tool trained on it did worse there.

questions.6.options.1.text.source: Why the tool did better with photos from India

questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. With so few photos from India, the tool did worse there, not better. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.6.options.2.text.source: Why people in India took fewer photos

questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The numbers show what is in the collection. They do not show how many photos people took. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.7.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. At the made-up Stonebay market, a tool names fish from photos. It names river fish well, but it often gets sea fish wrong. Almost all of its training photos show river fish.

questions.7.question.source: What would most likely help the tool?

questions.7.options.0.text.source: Add more photos of river fish

questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. It already knows river fish well. More of the same kind will not fill the gap. Look back at Lesson 8.

questions.7.options.1.text.source: Add labelled photos of sea fish

questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Its training data does not represent sea fish. Labelled photos of sea fish can fill that gap.

questions.7.options.2.text.source: Use the tool only when it is sunny

questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The light is not the problem. The problem is what its training photos show. Look back at Lesson 8.

results.high.source: Well done. You can see the people, the planet and the languages behind AI tools.

results.middle.source: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.

results.low.source: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 5–8, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
